A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MedMCP-Calc benchmark and CalcMate models. The complete main texts and appendices support comparison, and corresponding equations, figures, tables, schemas, and prompts can be matched despite pagination and numbering changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 23 comparison models and CalcMate on 118 clinical tasks, including performance scores, tool-use measurements, and extra-calculator analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds comparisons of data-construction and result-extraction models, alongside a detailed GPT-5 failure case.

M1.justification: The benchmark pipeline and CalcMate's scenario-planning and tool-augmentation approach remain intact. However, new Appendix A.4 attributes SQL training traces to Qwen and restricts GPT-5 to planning, whereas Section 4.3 in both versions attributes SQL data to GPT-5. The PDFs do not establish whether this procedure changed or the new description is erroneous.

E1.justification: Both versions retain 118 clinical tasks across four domains, the same MIMIC-IV-derived environment, and the same calculator pool. The added case study and validation checks examine existing tasks, construction inputs, and trajectories. Appendix A.4 supplies training-set composition without establishing expanded coverage.

E2.justification: The main leaderboard's comparison models are unchanged. Appendices C.1–C.2 introduce GPT-5.2 as an evaluated comparator for GPT-OSS-120B calculator deduplication and DeepSeek-V3.1 scenario assignment and result extraction; GPT-5.2 is not added to the clinical-task leaderboard.

E3.justification: v2 adds auxiliary validation protocols using 100 positive and 100 negative calculator pairs, 600 randomly sampled calculator–scenario pairs, and extraction comparisons on 20 sampled tasks under identical prompts. These introduce sampling designs and agreement/correlation metrics. The main evaluation protocol is retained; the newly documented 80-round limit and training configuration do not establish changed settings.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing model, domain, and tool-use analyses, v2 adds trajectory-based discussion of tool efficiency, an ARDS failure breakdown and worked example in B.4–B.5, and validation of construction-model and extractor choices in C.1–C.2. These substantially expand the investigation of failure mechanisms and pipeline reliability.

E5.justification: The new validation studies introduce Cohen's kappa and Pearson/Spearman correlation reporting, with MAD for differences between extracted scores. This adds statistical assessment of inter-model consistency. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the main benchmark results.

E6.justification: New results include 95% deduplication agreement, scenario-assignment kappa of 0.855, and 85.4% overall extraction agreement, with weaker SQL-field agreement (Tables 8–10). Table 7 reports five correct calculator selections and two correct results out of ten for the ARDS case. Tables 2–3 and Figure 3 retain their results; the conclusion corrects 33.97% to 33.92%, matching Table 2.

T1.justification: The POMDP formalization in Section 3.1 and all four metric formulas in Appendix A.2 are unchanged. The added empirical agreement statistics do not introduce new mathematical definitions, proofs, or theoretical results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: realistic MCP-based medical-calculator evaluation, limitations revealed across 23 models, and CalcMate's claimed open-source performance advantage. The conclusion's numerical correction does not change these claims' scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations distinguishing coordinated tool use from redundant looping, attributes ARDS failures to planning omissions, retrieval problems, and calculator confusion, and argues for the reliability and cost effectiveness of construction and extraction models. B.3 also moderates its description of GPT-5's ranking. The existing limitations remain unchanged, while new claims of statistical equivalence and ranking stability exceed what the reported agreement evidence alone establishes.

D1.justification: New A.3–A.4 disclose the complete ReAct prompt, 80-round limit, training-data composition, and detailed fine-tuning configuration: one epoch, learning rate 1e-5, 150,000-token sequences, batching, distributed-training settings, and GPU allocations. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation. Training-data provenance remains inconsistent between A.4 and Section 4.3.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds an LLM Agents discussion covering reinforcement learning, reflection, multi-agent systems, API tools, coding and GUI agents, and EHR-MCP. Numerous corresponding works are newly cited, substantially broadening research context. The existing MCP-benchmark and medical-calculator positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained, with localized wording corrections and added cross-references. New appendix subsections organize configuration, training, failure analysis, and validation material; the existing implementation subsections become C.3–C.5. This is an extension of the established structure rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Six new tables present case inputs, ground-truth workflow, GPT-5 outputs, and validation statistics (Tables 5–10), substantially expanding tabular support. The original nine schema tables are retained as Tables 11–19. Figures 1–3 and the main table designs are preserved, with surrounding material reflowed.

improvement.justification: The added ReAct and training details, pipeline checks, and worked failure case improve reproducibility and scrutiny of the evaluation. These gains are limited by conflicting SQL-training provenance and unsupported inferences from agreement to statistical equivalence and preserved model rankings. Overall, v2 provides a useful but bounded quality improvement over the retained main evidence.
